title: TLS 1.3 & X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Guide
description: A comprehensive course on asymmetric cryptography, TLS 1.3 handshakes, X.509 certificate chains, OpenSSL automation, ACME certbot renewals, and Go mTLS.
body: Master Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). Learn TLS 1.3 1-RTT handshake mechanics, certificate authority chains (Root CA -> Intermediate CA -> Leaf Cert), OpenSSL CLI command usage, and mutual TLS (mTLS) enforcement.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: TLS 1.3 1-RTT Handshake Architecture
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Slow First Connection on a Mobile Network

On a high-latency mobile connection, every network round trip costs real, perceptible time. TLS 1.2 required two full round trips before any application data could flow: one to agree on a cipher suite, a second to actually exchange keys. On a 200ms-latency connection, that's 400ms spent just setting up encryption, before the first byte of the actual page loads.

### 1-RTT: Combining Cipher Agreement and Key Exchange

TLS 1.3's key structural change is that the client doesn't wait to be told which key-exchange group the server will use — it guesses the most likely one and sends its ECDHE key share **in the same message** as its cipher suite proposal:

```text
  TLS 1.2 (2-RTT)                          TLS 1.3 (1-RTT)

  Client                Server             Client                Server
    │── ClientHello ────►│                   │── ClientHello +    │
    │                     │                   │   key_share ──────►│
    │◄── ServerHello ─────│                   │                     │
    │◄── Certificate ─────│                   │◄── ServerHello +   │
    │◄── ServerKeyExch ───│                   │    Certificate +    │
    │◄── ServerHelloDone ─│                   │    key_share +      │
    │                     │                   │    Finished ────────│
    │── ClientKeyExch ───►│                   │                     │
    │── ChangeCipherSpec ►│                   │── Finished ─────────►│
    │── Finished ────────►│                   │                     │
    │                     │                   │  Application data   │
    │  Application data   │                   │  can flow after     │
    │  after 2 round      │                   │  ONE round trip     │
    │  trips              │                   │                     │
```

Because the client already sent its key share up front, the server can derive the shared secret and start encrypting its response — including the certificate — in the very same flight. The client only needs one more message (`Finished`) to complete the handshake, cutting setup time roughly in half.

### What Changed Under the Hood

| TLS 1.2 | TLS 1.3 |
| :--- | :--- |
| Cipher suite negotiated, THEN key exchange happens in a second round trip | Client proactively sends a key share guess; server responds with everything needed to finish in one round trip |
| Supports weak/legacy ciphers (RC4, static RSA key exchange, CBC-mode ciphers vulnerable to padding oracle attacks) | Only forward-secret AEAD cipher suites (e.g. `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`) — no legacy fallback |
| Renegotiation handshake used for various purposes, source of several CVEs | Renegotiation removed entirely; replaced by narrower, safer mechanisms |

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: The 1-RTT handshake isn't just a latency optimization — dropping support for weak cipher suites and renegotiation simultaneously closed off entire classes of historical TLS vulnerabilities (BEAST, POODLE, Logjam) by making them structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: OpenSSL CLI Certificate Management Cheatsheet
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: Debugging a Handshake Failure with No Visibility

A service refuses TLS connections with a cryptic client-side error. Before reaching for application logs, the fastest way to isolate whether the problem is the certificate, the key, or the negotiated protocol itself is to inspect and test the handshake directly with `openssl`.

```bash
# Generate RSA 4096-bit private key
openssl genrsa -out server.key 4096

# Generate Certificate Signing Request (CSR)
openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr -subj "/CN=api.geekgully.local"

# Generate self-signed certificate (dev/test only — never for production)
openssl x509 -req -days 365 -in server.csr -signkey server.key -out server.crt

# Inspect a certificate's fields: subject, issuer, validity window, SANs
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -text

# Verify a leaf certificate against a chain of intermediates and a root
openssl verify -CAfile root-ca.pem -untrusted intermediate-ca.pem server.crt

# Connect to a live server and print its full certificate chain + negotiated
# TLS version/cipher — the single most useful command for debugging a
# handshake failure in production
openssl s_client -connect api.geekgully.local:443 -servername api.geekgully.local -showcerts

# Check exactly how many days remain before a certificate expires
openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -enddate
```

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: `openssl s_client -showcerts` reproduces exactly what a browser sees during the handshake — if it shows only one certificate instead of the expected leaf+intermediate pair, that confirms the "incomplete chain" misconfiguration from Lesson 1.2 before you've touched a single line of server configuration.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Automating Certificate Renewal with ACME / Certbot
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: An Expired Certificate That Took Down Checkout at 2 AM

A certificate issued manually 90 days ago expires silently over a long weekend. No human was watching a calendar reminder, and the on-call engineer wakes up to every browser refusing to connect to checkout — a fully preventable outage caused entirely by manual certificate lifecycle management.

### ACME: Certificate Issuance as an Automated Protocol

The ACME protocol (used by Let's Encrypt and others) lets a server prove domain ownership and receive a signed certificate entirely via automation, with no human in the loop:

```bash
# One-time: obtain a certificate via the HTTP-01 challenge (Certbot proves
# domain ownership by serving a token at a well-known URL on port 80)
certbot certonly --standalone -d api.geekgully.local --agree-tos -m ops@geekgully.local

# Certbot installs a systemd timer / cron job automatically, but the
# underlying renewal command it runs twice daily is:
certbot renew --quiet

# Certificates are only actually renewed when within 30 days of expiry —
# `renew` is safe to run frequently since it's a no-op otherwise
```

```text
  Cron/systemd timer (twice daily)
            │
            ▼
   certbot renew --quiet
            │
            ▼
   ┌───────────────────────┐   > 30 days left    ┌─────────────┐
   │ Check cert expiry for  │ ──────────────────► │  No-op       │
   │ every managed domain   │                     └─────────────┘
   └───────────┬───────────┘
               │  <= 30 days left
               ▼
   ┌───────────────────────┐
   │ ACME HTTP-01/DNS-01     │  proves domain ownership again,
   │ challenge + reissue     │  gets a fresh certificate
   └───────────┬───────────┘
               │
               ▼
   ┌───────────────────────┐
   │ --deploy-hook reloads   │  e.g. `systemctl reload nginx` —
   │ the web server          │  picks up the new cert with zero downtime
   └───────────────────────┘
```

For a service that can't bind port 80 (the HTTP-01 challenge's requirement), the **DNS-01 challenge** proves ownership by requiring a TXT record be published instead — the mechanism of choice for wildcard certificates (`*.geekgully.local`) and internal services with no public HTTP endpoint at all.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: The `--deploy-hook` is what actually prevents the 2 AM outage — issuing a new certificate does nothing until the running service reloads it, so the renewal automation is only complete once it also reloads or restarts the process consuming the certificate.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.3: Enforcing Mutual TLS (mTLS) in Go Backend Microservices
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Zero-Trust Requirement With No Enforcement

A security policy states that internal services must mutually authenticate over TLS. In practice, `tls.Config{}` is left at its defaults, which only verifies the SERVER's certificate to the client — the server never asks the client to prove who it is. The policy exists on paper but nothing in the code actually enforces it.

### Enforcing mTLS with `RequireAndVerifyClientCert`

```go
package pki

import (
	"crypto/tls"
	"crypto/x509"
	"net/http"
	"os"
)

func NewMTLSServer(certFile, keyFile, caFile, addr string, handler http.Handler) (*http.Server, error) {
	serverCert, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair(certFile, keyFile)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	caCert, err := os.ReadFile(caFile)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	caPool := x509.NewCertPool()
	caPool.AppendCertsFromPEM(caCert)

	tlsConfig := &tls.Config{
		Certificates: []tls.Certificate{serverCert},
		ClientCAs:    caPool,
		ClientAuth:   tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert, // the enforcement the policy actually needed
		MinVersion:   tls.VersionTLS13,
	}

	return &http.Server{Addr: addr, Handler: handler, TLSConfig: tlsConfig}, nil
}
```

### `tls.ClientAuthType` Options — Choosing the Right Enforcement Level

| Value | Behavior | When to use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `NoClientCert` | Default — client cert never requested | Public-facing endpoints |
| `RequestClientCert` | Requested but NOT required or verified | Never — silently insecure, easy to misconfigure into thinking mTLS is active |
| `RequireAnyClientCert` | A cert is required, but not verified against any CA | Rare; doesn't actually authenticate identity |
| `VerifyClientCertIfGiven` | Verified if present, but connection allowed without one | Gradual migration period only, never steady-state |
| `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` | Required AND verified against `ClientCAs` | The correct setting for zero-trust internal service-to-service traffic |

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: `RequestClientCert` is the most dangerous option in this list precisely because it looks like it's doing something — a service using it will happily accept connections from callers presenting no certificate at all, giving a false sense of enforcement that `RequireAndVerifyClientCert` alone actually delivers.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.4: Knowledge Check — TLS & PKI
lessons.body:
**Question 1:** Why does TLS 1.3 achieve a handshake in one round trip while TLS 1.2 needs two?

A) TLS 1.3 uses a faster network protocol underneath
B) The client proactively sends a guessed key share alongside its ClientHello, so the server can derive the shared secret and respond with everything needed to finish in a single additional round trip
C) TLS 1.3 skips certificate verification entirely
D) TLS 1.3 doesn't support forward secrecy, which removes a step

**Correct answer: B.** TLS 1.2 negotiates the cipher suite first, then performs key exchange in a separate round trip; TLS 1.3 collapses both into the initial exchange by having the client send its key share speculatively.

---

**Question 2:** A server sends only its leaf certificate, without the intermediate CA certificate that signed it. What's the most likely symptom?

A) The connection is faster because there's less data to send
B) Clients that don't already have the specific intermediate CA cached will fail to build a trust chain to a root they recognize, showing a certificate error even though the leaf certificate itself is valid and unexpired
C) The server will refuse to start
D) OCSP stapling stops working, but the chain still validates fine

**Correct answer: B.** Browsers need the full path from leaf to a trusted root; without the intermediate, most clients cannot bridge that gap even if they'd trust the root the intermediate ultimately chains to.

---

**Question 3:** Why is `tls.ClientAuthType` set to `RequestClientCert` considered more dangerous than simply leaving it at the default `NoClientCert`?

A) It has worse performance
B) It requests a client certificate but never requires or verifies one, which can create a false impression that mTLS is enforced when in fact any client — with or without a valid certificate — is still accepted
C) It's deprecated and no longer functions in modern Go versions
D) It only works with self-signed certificates

**Correct answer: B.** A setting that appears to engage client certificate logic but doesn't actually enforce or verify it is a classic "looks secure but isn't" misconfiguration — worse than an honestly-absent control because it can pass a superficial code review.
